item.content:encoded: When dealing with an area of the ocean, the distances should be in Nautical Miles (Nm). 1 Nm equals roughly 1.9 Km, or 1.15 miles. The nautical mile is used by sea and air navigators worldwide because of its convenience when working with charts. A nautical mile is nearly equal to a minute of latitude on a chart, so a distance measured with a chart divider can be roughly converted to nautical miles using the chart's latitude scale.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Though the wreck is designated SCP-473, the anomalies associated with it are believed to be caused by an Inca relic located within. The unconfirmed relic is designated SCP-473-1. Phenomena encountered by ships approaching SCP-473 include disembodied voices (which may have knowledge of Foundation personnel and operations), and minor physical disturbances such as unidentified vibrations and impacts on the ship. Personnel in the area are advised to confirm the physical presence of anyone they are in communication with and to ignore any voices that have no discernible source. Craft entering SCP-473's Prohibited Zone may be disassembled from the inside due to its effects.

Speculation doesn't belong here. I would say that the anomalies may be attributable to an unconfirmed relic. Actually, upon thinking about it, I probably wouldn't even say that. That requires assumptions based on assumptions. I'd possibly just mention what was supposedly on board the ship at the time it sank and not present its cargo as possibly contributing to the effect since there's no way to actually know.

You don't actually say much about its effects until the logs. Insert oft-recited rant about the important stuff being in the description and how if the reader has to read the secondary materials to know what they're dealing with, you're doing it wrong.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I agree that the overtness of the "Inca death god" angle is not ideal, but I'm not sure how it could be changed to fix that. Expunging the bit about "He said Supai was their new God, the god of the dead. He said Supai would be our God, in time." might help - it's a little corny.

More nitpicky suggestions:
- "My friend Mike told me…" needs a tone-related tweak, to something more like "Mike █████ told me" or "Seaman █████ told me". This is a Foundation naval officer, not a ten-year-old.
- In the quoted correspondence, "girl's" should be " girls' ", if you're talking about two girls' possessions. If you're not, it should be rephrased to make that clear.
- I'm not sure whether "early 1500's" refers to early in the period 1500-1509 or 1500-1599. If the latter, "early 16th century" would fit the desired tone better.
- "GPS coordinates" is a really awkward phrase, given the fact that GPS systems don't use any distinct set of coordinates. Trimming the "GPS" and changing the blackboxes to the correct length to accomodate a ██º██'██"N ███º██'██"W coordinate format would be good.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The approach here is a little indelicate. If ever an article needed show-not-tell writing, this is it- subtlety is your friend. Just dumping an Inca death god rock in our laps 1/3 of the way in ruined any hope of build up. I'd recommend some shuffling- maybe even remove the "Note: Though the wreck is…" paragraph and rely on the existing email to point in that direction, maybe even add in one or two more SMALL bits of correspondence.

The one other specific recommendation I can make is to remove the parenthetical explanations of the three colored "zones" around the wreck- Foundation jargon can be a lot more interesting without explicit definition. Additionally, I might recommend using yellow, red, and black / dark / something more ominous instead of yellow, orange, and red. Perhaps even ???, kill, and quarantine if you prefer to be explicit. If you use color names without parentheticals but still want to make clear that there are deaths in the second zone, you might add some note about proper disposal of bodies from that area to make sure they don't end up too close to the wreck.
